value.overview: The Brown Violetear (Colibri delphinae) is a medium-sized hummingbird of humid mountain forests and woodland edges in Central and South America. It is named for the broad violet patch behind the eye, which is especially noticeable when the bird turns its head in sunlight. Although often associated with forested uplands, it may also visit plantations, gardens, clearings, and flowering trees. Costa Rica lies near the northern part of its range and supports local populations in suitable highland habitats.
value.classification: The Brown Violetear belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Colibri. It is one of the four recognized violetears.
value.identification: This hummingbird is about 11 to 12 centimeters long. Adults are mainly olive-green to bronzy green above, with a grayish or brownish breast and belly. The most distinctive feature is the large violet patch on the sides of the head behind the eyes. The bill is fairly straight and dark, and the tail is dusky bronze or greenish. Its appearance can vary with lighting, and the violet ear patch may be difficult to see when the bird is facing away.
value.rangeHabitat: The Brown Violetear occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America, including parts of the Andes. In Costa Rica, it is a local bird of humid and wet highlands, especially in forested mountain regions and adjacent foothills. It uses montane evergreen forest, forest borders, second growth, shaded coffee plantations, gardens, and other areas with abundant flowers. Records are generally associated with middle and upper elevations, although its local distribution can vary with season and food availability.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally regarded as a resident or partly resident species in Costa Rica. Individuals may make local or elevational movements, following flowering plants and changing food supplies, but it is not known as a long-distance migrant there.
value.breeding: The breeding season varies across its broad range and may be influenced by rainfall and local flowering conditions. Like other hummingbirds, the female builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually from plant fibers, moss, and other soft material, often on a slender branch. She incubates the eggs and raises the young without assistance from the male. Nest placement and timing in Costa Rica can vary among elevations and habitats.
value.dietFeeding: The Brown Violetear feeds mainly on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and epiphytes. It also captures small insects and other arthropods, which provide important protein, especially during breeding. It may defend productive flowers or feeding areas from other hummingbirds, but it can also forage widely through forest edges and gardens. Flowers with tubular or exposed nectar are commonly used, and the species may visit feeders where these are available.
value.behavior: This species is active and agile, moving rapidly between flowers and often hovering briefly while feeding. It commonly perches on exposed twigs or branches between feeding bouts. Brown Violetears can be territorial around rich flower sources and may chase other hummingbirds, although several individuals may occur in the same general area when food is plentiful. Their calls are sharp, high-pitched notes, and their plumage can appear quite different depending on light and viewing angle.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established, although habitat loss may be causing local declines in parts of its range.
conservation.threats: Potential threats include clearing and fragmentation of humid montane forest, loss of flowering plants, agricultural expansion, and degradation of forest edges and highland habitats. These pressures may be particularly important where populations are small or isolated.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining mountain forest and maintain connected forest edges, flowering shrubs, native trees, and epiphytes. In Costa Rica, shade-grown farms and gardens can support the species when they retain native vegetation and avoid excessive pesticide use. Protecting flowering plants throughout the year helps provide both nectar and insect prey.
